title: Searching for a Controller by Trying It: A Pole on a Cart, Four Gains, and Random Changes Kept When They Help

questions.question: Why can the Q table of 39-03 not be used to balance a pole on a cart?
options: The state is continuous, so there is no cell for every state
The cart has only two actions
The table would be too accurate
questions.explanation: A table needs a cell per state; a controller with a few numbers does not.

questions.question: With every gain zero, how long did the pole balance, and after 300 tries of random search?
questions.explanation: From falling at once to balancing almost the whole limit of 500 steps.

questions.question: From 100 starts the search never saw, how long did the found gains balance?
questions.explanation: It learned the task, not the twenty starts it was scored on.

questions.question: How many trial runs did the search take?
questions.explanation: 300 tries of 20 runs each, every one a pole that may fall on a real cart.

questions.question: When should a controller be learned by trial rather than designed from the equations?
options: When the equations are not known or not to be trusted
Only when the controller has one gain
questions.explanation: With good equations, design (phase 14); use learning to check or tune.

questions.question: Why are the found gains tested on starts the search never used?
options: To check it learned the task and not the particular starts it was scored on
Because the search used no starts
questions.explanation: Scored on fixed starts, a search can fit them; held-out starts say whether it generalises.
